extracted.intended_audience: Ohio and Kentucky voters; general 19th-century U.S. electorate interested in the slavery question
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century political oration arguing against 'popular sovereignty' and for preventing the spread/nationalization of slavery; addresses multiple local audiences and exposes logical consequences of opponents' positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consequences test
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply an opponent's principle to its logical conclusions to reveal unacceptable outcomes (e.g., Douglas's popular sovereignty logically leads to reopening the African slave trade and nationalizing slavery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln repeatedly extends Douglas's 'popular sovereignty' to its endpoints: if people in Territories may have slaves because they want them, then people in slave States may buy slaves in Africa; if the Constitution 'carries' slavery into Territories, it would be carried into States. Use this method to show practical and moral consequences of an abstract principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual/interpretive fidelity of judicial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether a court decision merely declares a want of power or affirmatively recognizes a right (Lincoln's reading of Dred Scott: it does more than negative declarations; it 'affirm[s] the right of property in a slave' in the Constitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at the precise language used by the Court: does it state absence of power only, or does it affirm that slave property is woven into the Constitution? If affirmative language exists, treat the decision as establishing, not merely limiting, a constitutional guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as the basis of political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat public sentiment as the foundational force in a popular government; evaluate how speech or doctrine shapes that sentiment (Lincoln: 'public opinion in this country is everything').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a politician's rhetoric 'moulds public opinion' toward a particular end, and whether that shaping serves an interest (e.g., Douglas molding Northern opinion to favor Southern slavery). Consider long-term effects of such molding on law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency vs. tactical ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether a political actor is sincere in their stated principles or uses ambiguity to retain broad support (Douglas 'never says your institution of slavery is wrong' to keep Northern support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate statements for deliberate non-commitment (e.g., 'I do not care whether slavery is voted up or voted down') and weigh tactical advantages gained by avoiding moral judgment. Call out when silence or equivocation is used to 'inveigle' support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry/analogy checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Test claimed distinctions by proposing symmetrical cases (e.g., if Territory residents may have slaves because they want them, why may not Georgians buy slaves in Africa?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force the opponent to justify why two apparently parallel situations should be treated differently; use analogies and symmetry to expose arbitrary or untenable distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical expectation and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use historical facts and expectations at the founding (e.g., expectations about abolishing the foreign slave trade and restraining slavery in the Territories; Ordinance of 1787) to evaluate the legitimacy of present claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite contemporary historical practices and public expectations to challenge modern reinterpretations (argue that founding-era sentiment expected restriction of slavery spread and abolition of slave trade, therefore claims of constitutional compromise are unfounded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral framing vs. economic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish moral condemnation from economic or 'dollars and cents' treatment of human beings; identify when opponents reduce persons to property or 'brutes' to justify policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose arguments that relegate human beings to economic objects (Lincoln contrasts moral condemnation of slavery with Douglas's tendencies to treat the negro 'as a matter of dollars and cents' and 'among reptiles and crocodiles'). Show how economic framing enables injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of founding texts in civic argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate and contest claims about the meaning of the Declaration of Independence and Constitution (e.g., whether 'all men' included negroes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track shifts in public and partisan interpretation of founding documents; call for fidelity to broader principles when opponents reinterpret texts to exclude groups. Use evidence of prior common understanding to rebut novel exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-targeted persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor arguments to specific local audiences' concerns and incentives (Lincoln addresses Kentuckians on why Douglas is 'for you' and Ohioans on why they should reject him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speaking to varied constituencies, highlight how an opponent's position benefits or harms the local audience; emphasize strategic advantages (e.g., Douglas gives slaveholders a 'hold upon the North').

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose rhetorical devices that degrade opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and criticize rhetorical moves that dehumanize or degrade (e.g., calling the negro a 'brute' or comparing him to reptiles) as part of a campaign to 'debauch public opinion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out language that shifts moral perception downward and warn that continued use prepares the public to accept worse policies (revival of the slave trade, territorial slave codes, new judicial decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and social harm argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight tangible harms slavery imposes on nonslaveholders (e.g., slave labor injures 'the mass of the white men' by depressing free labor conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement moral arguments with concrete material consequences to broaden appeal and show self-interest of potential allies (use local economic examples: profitably-cultivated crops, climate suitability arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out strategic political benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a politician's positions are designed to secure support across regions and thereby provide strategic advantage to a particular interest (Douglas 'constantly moulds public opinion' to give Southern interests hold on the North).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze political positioning for whether it actually serves the opposing group's long-term aims; show how rhetoric that appears neutral can function instrumentally to sustain an interest.
